HOW DO YOU IDENTIFY A GOOD MANAGER? ∗ B EN W EIDMANN J OSEPH V ECCI F ARAH S AID S ONIA B HALOTRA A CHYUTA A DHVARYU A NANT N YSHADHAM J ORGE T AMAYO D AVID D EMING We introduce and validate a novel approach to identifying good managers. In a preregistered lab experiment, we causally identify managerial contributions by randomly assigning managers to teams and controlling for individual skill. We Þnd that manager contributions are crucial for team success, and that peo- ple who self-select into management roles perform worse than randomly assigned managers. Managerial performance is strongly predicted by economic decision- making skill but not by demographic characteristics. Two validation studies sup- port our experimental results. Participants who succeed in the lab receive more real-world promotions and, in a separate study of retail store managers, skill mea- sures strongly predict store sales. A one standard deviation increase in manager quality increases annual per store sales by US$4.1 million (25% increase). Se- lecting managers on skills rather than demographic characteristics or the desire to lead could substantially improve organizational performance. I NTRODUCTION Management matters greatly for economic performance ( Bloom and Van Reenen 2007 ; Bloom, Sadun, and Van Reenen 2016 ; Bruhn, Karlan, and Schoar 2018 ; Giorcelli 2019 ; Gosnell, List, and Metcalfe 2020 ; Metcalfe, Sollaci, and Syverson 2023b ). There are large, persistent productivity differences between man- agers within Þrms and across countries ( Lazear, Shaw, and Stanton 2015 ; Bender et al. 2018 ; Adhvaryu, Nyshadham, and Tamayo 2023 ; Metcalfe, Sollaci, and Syverson 2023a ). Good man- agers increase productivity through many channels, including monitoring performance, training and motivating staff, and re- allocating workers to better roles or job tasks ( Fenizia 2022 ; Metcalfe, Sollaci, and Syverson 2023a ; Minni 2023 ; Adhvaryu, Nyshadham, and Tamayo 2023 ; Dessein et al. 2024 ; Benson and Shaw 2025 ). How do Þrms identify good managers? In practice, Þrms rely heavily on the judgment of existing managers, which suffers from well-known biases ( Kahneman and Klein 2009 ; Hoffman, Kahn, and Li 2018 ; Chamorro-Premuzic 2019 ; Feld et al. 2022 ). Firms can also select managers based on personality traits and cognitive ability. Research has shown that these characteristics exhibit pos- itive associations with manager performance in the Þeld ( Judge et al. 2002 ; Judge, Colbert, and Ilies 2004 ; Javalagi, Newman, and Li 2024 ). Existing research on manager selection suffers from two practical limitations. First, managers are not randomly assigned to teams, which makes it difÞcult to causally identify managerial performance. 1 Second, managers in the Þeld are a highly nonran- dom sample of the population. This may lead to incorrect infer- ences about the characteristics that truly improve performance. For example, Benson, Li, and Shue (2019) Þnd that sales man- agers are selected based on their performance as line workers, that is, according to the Peter principle. 2 Promotions based on the Peter principle can induce a negative correlation between 1. A relatively small number of high-quality Þeld studies use manager rota- tion for identiÞcation ( Lazear, Shaw, and Stanton 2015 ; Wells 2020 ; Fenizia 2022 ; Giardili, Ramdas, and Williams 2023 ; Metcalfe, Sollaci, and Syverson 2023a ; Minni 2023 ). We follow this quasi-experimental approach in our Þeld study of retail managers (see Section IV ). 2. The Peter principle states that employees are promoted to their level of incompetence ( Peter and Hull 1969 ).
HOW DO YOU IDENTIFY A GOOD MANAGER? 1583 a workerÕs performance and their subsequent performance as a manager, even though the causal effect of increasing worker skills among managers is likely positive ( Benson, Li, and Shue 2019 ). We introduce a novel method for identifying effective man- agers, using a large preregistered lab experiment ( n = 555). First, we causally identify managerial contributions by randomly as- signing each manager to multiple teams and controlling for task- speciÞc performance of managers and workers, which isolates management skill from productive capacity. 3 We design a collab- orative task that emulates real-world team production by requir- ing managers to coordinate, monitor, and motivate workers. Over the course of the experiment we randomly assign each manager to four different three-person teams. Intuitively, good managers con- sistently cause their teams to produce more than the sum of their parts. We Þnd that the impact of good management is relatively large: a one standard deviation increase in managerial skill im- proves team performance by 0.22 standard deviations conditional on the productive skills of all workers including the manager. To put these Þgures into context, we Þnd that overall manager qual- ity matters about as much to team performance as the combined productive capacity of workers. Second, we investigate whether people who self-select into management roles typically perform well on the job. After de- scribing the tasks and compensation structure of the managers and workers, we elicit the preference of participants to be a man- ager on a 1Ð10 scale. Half of all groups were then randomly as- signed to a self-promotion treatment where participants with the strongest preferences to be a manager were given the role. The other half of managers were drawn randomly from the partici- pant pool. 4 We Þnd that teams with self-promoted managers per- form 0.1 standard deviations less well than teams with randomly assigned managers, a gap that is roughly equivalent to being as- signed a manager with a one standard deviation lower ßuid IQ score. Exploratory analyses suggest that the underperformance of self-promoted managers may be related to overconÞdence. We 3. A related approach is used by Weidmann and Deming (2021) to identify workers who are good team players. We build on this method by introducing hier- archical teams, developing a new collaborative management task, and validating our approach with Þeld data. 4. Each participant was only given one role throughout the experiment.
1584 THE QUARTERLY JOURNAL OF ECONOMICS Þnd that people who express a preference for managerial roles overestimate their social skills relative to an objective test of emotional perceptiveness called the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test (RMET). 5 Among self-promoted managers, we also Þnd a negative relationship between self-reported people skills and managerial performance. Conversely, randomly selected man- agers do not overestimate their social skills, and we Þnd no nega- tive relationship between self-reported people skills and manage- rial performance. What characteristics do predict managerial success in the lab? To answer this question, we focus on the sample of lottery managers as the associations between manager performance and manager characteristics in the self-promoted treatment arm are moderated by the Þlter of self-selection. We identify two consis- tent predictors of managerial contributions: economic decision- making skill and ßuid intelligence. 6 These relationships are ro- bust to a wide range of controls, including age, gender, education, work experience, emotional perceptiveness, and personality traits including risk preferences. No other characteristics strongly pre- dict managerial performance. We conduct two separate Þeld studies to validate our exper- imental results and evaluate their economic importance. First, we use publicly available LinkedIn data on our lab experiment participants to test whether managerial performance measured in the lab corresponds to meaningful differences in actual career progression. Although our sample is limited to early-career work- ers (mean age = 27.5 years; mean work experience = 4.9 years) we Þnd that a one standard deviation increase in the lab mea- sure of managerial performance is associated with 0.16 more real-world promotions per year ( p < .001, n = 73; base rate of 0.25 promotions per year). The association is robust to controls for ßuid intelligence, age, gender, ethnicity, and personality, sug- gesting that our experimental measure of managerial skill cap- 5. We also Þnd that self-promoters systematically overestimate their perfor- mance and abilities, consistent with prior evidence that managers and executives tend to exhibit overconÞdence ( Malmendier and Tate 2015 ; Huffman, Raymond, and Shvets 2022 ). 6. Economic decision-making skill is deÞned and operationalized in Caplin et al. (2024) and focuses on the ability to strategically allocate scarce attention in a resource allocation task. Caplin et al. (2024) Þnds that this skill is a strong predictor of labor earnings among full-time workers in the United States and Den- mark, particularly in managerial roles.
HOW DO YOU IDENTIFY A GOOD MANAGER? 1585 tures something predictive of career progression above and be- yond traditional predictors, such as education, intelligence, or de- mographic factors. Second, we examine the role of managerial skills in a Þrm set- ting, where managers have repeated, long-term interactions with staff. We recruit a sample of grocery store managers employed by a multibillion-dollar retail Þrm in South America. Each store manager completed a set of three skill assessments that matched the skills assessed before the lab experiment: economic decision- making skill, ßuid intelligence, and emotional perceptiveness. We link these test scores to detailed data on store performance and sales over a 28-month period. The Þeld setting is analogous to our lab experiment in sev- eral ways. Importantly, the middle managers we study have sim- ilar core responsibilities to managers in our lab setting: they del- egate tasks to frontline workers, motivate staff, monitor perfor- mance, and address potential bottlenecks (e.g., inventory stock- outs). As the stores share standardized practices and procedures, manager mobility across stores represents a nonrandom analogue of our repeated randomization procedure. Our Þeld setting there- fore provides a nonexperimental measure of managerial perfor- mance that can be used to quantify the value of middle managers and to examine whether the broad skills that predict manager contributions in the lab also predict performance in the Þeld. Using an event-study design, we estimate that a good man- ager (deÞned as being one standard deviation better in terms of managerial Þxed effect) improves annual per store sales by US$4.1 million (25%). This improvement is broadly in line with empirical estimates from other industries, which have linked a one standard deviation improvement in management quality to performance improvements of 10%Ð22% ( Wells 2020 ; Fenizia 2022 ; Giardili, Ramdas, and Williams 2023 ). 7 Notably, we Þnd that the strongest predictor of managerial performance is eco- nomic decision-making skill, which aligns with our experimental Þndings. A one standard deviation increase in economic decision- making is associated with a 0.19 standard deviation improvement in the performance of retail store managers ( p = .01). 7. Existing studies often report different metrics, such as the effect of mov- ing from the 25th to the 75th percentile in management quality; to make these comparable, we assume that managerial quality is normally distributed.
1586 THE QUARTERLY JOURNAL OF ECONOMICS We quantify the impact of different management selection regimes. Starting with evidence from the lab, results from the random assignment arm of the experiment suggest that selecting managers based on economic decision-making skill improves per- formance by 0.7 standard deviations relative to self-promotion. Selecting managers based on economic decision-making skill also yields signiÞcantly better manager performance than a random- assignment benchmark or selecting the most productive workers to be managers (by following the Peter principle). An analogous exercise using our Þeld data suggests that if new managers were hired based on their economic decision-making skills, annual per store sales would increase by US$2.6 million (16%). Last, we investigate what good managers do to help their teams succeed. We Þnd that good managers (i) monitor their workers to make sure bottlenecks are being addressed; (ii) match workers to the tasks that best Þt their skills; and (iii) keep work- ers motivated. Quantitatively, monitoring and motivation are more important than allocation, although all three are substan- tively important. In the experiment, good managersÑdeÞned as those scoring one standard deviation above average in terms of their managerial skillÑmake monitoring errors about half as of- ten as other managers. Similarly, in our Þeld study we demon- strate that good managersÑthose with strong economic decision- making skillsÑare more likely to successfully monitor stock and proactively avoid stockouts. Our article makes three main contributions. First, we de- velop a skills-based approach to assessing managerial talent that can prospectively identify people with strong managerial poten- tial. Our method complements the measures commonly used in economics and psychology to study managers. In economics, re- searchers measure managerial contributions by examining vari- ation in output when teams (or Þrms) are exposed to differ- ent managers ( Bertrand and Schoar 2003 ; Lazear, Shaw, and Stanton 2015 ; Janke, Propper, and Sadun 2024 ; Wells 2020 ; Fenizia 2022 ; Giardili, Ramdas, and Williams 2023 ; Metcalfe, Sollaci, and Syverson 2023a ; Minni 2023 ). Although these stud- ies have many strengths, they cannot be used prospectively to identify strong managers and have very demanding data require- ments. 8 Economists have successfully used interviews to capture 8. These approaches also suffer from the two main measurement issues noted above: nonrandom assignment of managers to teams and the limitation of only
HOW DO YOU IDENTIFY A GOOD MANAGER? 1587 differences in management practices across Þrms (e.g., Bloom and Van Reenen 2007 , 2010 ; Bloom, Sadun, and Van Reenen 2016 ). We complement this literature by showing how to identify the skill of individual managers, as distinct from Þrm practices. In industrial organization psychology, a related literature examines individual differences in managerial quality, relying on three main approaches to measurement: (i) self- or peer- reported managerial traits, such as personality or conÞdence (see Rotemberg and Saloner 2000 ; Judge et al. 2002 ; van den Steen 2005 ); (ii) self- or peer-reported managerial behaviors and lead- ership styles such as transformational, transactional, authentic, or identity leadership ( Bass and Avolio 2000 ; Walumbwa et al. 2008 ; Van Dick et al. 2018 ; Jensen et al. 2019 ; Beenen et al. 2021 ); and (iii) situational judgment tests in which participants are presented with hypothetical workplace scenarios and asked multiple-choice questions about the best way to respond ( Chan and Schmitt 2002 ; Whetzel and McDaniel 2009 ). Our approach complements this literature by focusing on performance-based measures of managerial skill. Second, we contribute to the empirical literature that quan- tiÞes the value of managers ( Bertrand and Schoar 2003 ; Lazear, Shaw, and Stanton 2015 ; Metcalfe, Sollaci, and Syverson 2023a ) by providing new evidence of the value of middle managers, an important group that has been relatively understudied compared to senior leaders ( Metcalfe, Sollaci, and Syverson 2023a ; Hoffman and Stanton 2024 ). Encouragingly, our lab and Þeld studies pro- duce similar results: in both cases the importance of manager quality and the overall quality of workers are roughly equiva- lent. 9 Similarly, the extent to which variation in manager quality is explained by skill measures and demographic characteristics is very similar in the lab and the Þeld. studying existing managers, who are a highly nonrandom sample. Our experiment relaxes both these constraints. 9. Lab results show that the total effect of a one standard deviation improve- ment in manager performance is 0.28, compared to 0.26 standard deviations for a one standard deviation improvement in the average productive skills of workers (a ratio of 1.1 × ). In the Þeld, we estimate that the impact on sales of a one stan- dard deviation improvement in manager quality increases sales 25%, compared to an 18% increase for a one standard deviation improvement in the average quality of workers across the store (a ratio of 1.4 × ). In related work, Lazear, Shaw, and Stanton (2015) estimate that across manager-worker dyads, worker effects are comparableÑbut somewhat larger thanÑmanager effects (by a ratio of 1.3 × ).
1588 THE QUARTERLY JOURNAL OF ECONOMICS Third, we extend two related literatures that examine the importance of leader selection mechanisms ( Berger et al. 2020 ; Erkal, Gangadharan, and Xiao 2022 ; Englmaier et al. 2024 ), as well as the characteristics and behaviors of good managers ( Judge et al. 2002 ; Judge, Colbert, and Ilies 2004 ; Javalagi, Newman, and Li 2024 ). We Þnd that the single best predictor of managerial per- formance in both the lab and the Þeld is a theoretically grounded measure of economic decision-making skill ( Caplin et al. 2024 ). Managerial effectiveness is not strongly predicted by personality and demographic traits. Notably, we also Þnd that people with a strong preference to be in charge perform marginally worse than managers appointed at random. These Þndings suggest that proactively engaging a wide set of candidates and screening them based on measures of skill could substantially improve manage- rial quality. The article proceeds as follows. Section II describes our ap- proach to identifying good managers in the lab and Section III re- ports our experimental Þndings. Section IV presents two tests of external validity and provides initial quantitative evidence about whether our experimental results are economically meani

Description of Experiment Our experiment was preregistered at the AEA RCT reg- istry. 12 Figure I presents an overview of the experiment. Our de- sign centers on a novel group task called the collaborative pro- duction task. Every time a man- ager is allocated to a team, they work on a parallel version of the collaborative production task. The experiment has two levels of randomization. We ran- domly assign participants to teams (repeatedly) and we randomly vary the way in which managers are selected. Before group testing began, all participants rated their pref- erence for being a manager on a scale of 1Ð10. Participants did not know how managers would be appointed when their managerial preferences were elicited. II.C. Group Task The group task was created for this experiment (see Online Appendix A.2 for a full discussion of design considerations). In the task, groups are required to work on three question modules: numerical, spatial, and analytical reasoning. The group receives a score for each module based on how many problems they have solved. They receive one point for correct answers and lose 0.5 points for incorrect answers. Each person in the team, including the manager, works on their own computer trying to solve a differ-
HOW DO YOU IDENTIFY A GOOD MANAGER? 1593 ent problem. Crucially, the manager decides who will be working on each module. The teamÕs overall score is given by the minimum module score, similar to the weakest-link coordination game where suc- cess hinges on effective collaboration (e.g., Hirshleifer 1983 ). 14 Each group of three sat next to each other in the lab, with the manager in the middle and a worker on either side. Before the task began, participants were informed that they were allowed to talk to each other, and teams communicated freely through- out the task. To avoid cross-team communication or interference, each team was separated from other teams by barriers and spare computer terminals. Overall, each group worked together for around 15 minutes. In the Þrst round of the experiment, participants received de- tailed instructions, including multiple comprehension checks. At the start of the task, participants were given time to introduce themselves and strategize about how they wanted to tackle the task. The timer began after the managers had entered their ini- tial task assignments. At this point the Þrst set of questions were shown. Groups worked on problems for eight minutes in total. This included two break periods of one minute, in which man- agers had time to regroup and motivate their team and/or re- strategize. 1. The Role of the Manager. We designed the task so that the manager role was both clearly differentiated from workers and essential for group success ( Brass 1984 ). Managers had multi- ple distinct responsibilities including delegation, monitoring, and motivation. First, managers were responsible for deciding who did what. Managers were allowed to delegate in any way they saw Þt, provided everyone (including the managers) was allocated to a module. Managers were able to allocate more than one per- son to any given module. For instance, if a manager allocated all three participants to the numerical module, each participant 14. This setup represents a scenario where team production relies on the con- tributions from all components of production. For instance, in producing a report the Þnal product is only complete when all sections are combined. Similarly, in manufacturing, a single absent or broken component can halt the entire produc- tion line. A manager is generally required to coordinate across teams to ensure the successful production of the combined product. The weakest-link setup is rel- evant for practical purposes because such coordination is common in economic production ( Riedl, Rohde, and Strobel 2016 ).
1594 THE QUARTERLY JOURNAL OF ECONOMICS would work on a different numerical problem. Allocations were dynamic, and managers could change their allocation at any time. Before the timer began, managers were presented with full infor- mation about each team memberÕs individual scores on the as- sessments of numerical, spatial, and analytical tests (conducted before the group session). Managers could review information about their teammatesÕ skill proÞle throughout the task. Man- agers also had constant access to a table describing the current allocation of tasks among their team. Second, managers monitored progress. Monitoring was es- pecially important given the weakest-link scoring rule. Only the managerÕs computer terminal showed the overall team score (i.e., the minimum module score). However, managers were not told which module had the lowest score. In contrast, workers are able to see the score of the module they are currently working on. 15 Consequently, managers needed to talk with their teammates to Þnd out which modules needed attention. Effective manage- ment required clear communication along with strong situational awareness as managers could, and often did, get swept up work- ing on the module they assigned to themselves. Last, managers motivated their teamÑan important role given that the tasks are both repetitive and cognitively demand- ing. As noted in Section II.E , the incentive structure meant that managers could not rely on Þnancial incentives to motivate work- ers. These responsibilities are common managerial duties, partic- ularly among middle managers. We deliberately focus on middle managersÑdistinct from senior leaders and CEOsÑbecause this group is relatively neglected in the literature ( Metcalfe, Sollaci, and Syverson 2023a ; Hoffman and Stanton 2024 ). II.D. Individual Tasks 1. Measuring Individual Productivity. Before group testing began, we assessed individualsÕ ability to solve problems on their own. The group task involved three types of problems (numeri- cal, spatial, and analytical reasoning), so participants were asked to complete individual assessments in these domains before- 15. If two workers are working on the same module, they will both see that moduleÕs score (rather than their individual contribution to the module).
HOW DO YOU IDENTIFY A GOOD MANAGER? 1595 hand. 16 These assessments provided a way to measure the pro- ductive capacity of any randomly assembled group (see Online Appendix A.1 for an example). For each of the three tests, participants were given four min- utes to solve as many problems as possible. They received 1 point for correct answers and lost 0.5 points for incorrect answers. Par- ticipants were aware of this scoring rule. We made this design choice to discourage guessing. 2. Broad Measures of Individual Skill. We measured three broad skills that might predict managerial performance: eco- nomic decision-making, ßuid intelligence, and emotional percep- tiveness. Importantly, we asked participants to complete these as- sessments well before they came to the lab for group testing. 17 We measured economic decision-making skill using the assignment game ( Caplin et al. 2024 ). The game requires participants to deal with an attentionally demanding numerical environment, under- stand comparative advantage intuitively, and avoid biases that undermine numerical decision-making (e.g., anchoring). Fluid in- telligence was measured with a set of Ravens Advanced Progres- sive Matrices, a widely used assessment of the ability to solve novel problems. We measured social skill using the RMET ( Baron- Cohen et al. 2001 ). The RMET assesses emotional perceptiveness by presenting participants with photos of faces, cropped so that only the eyes are visible. Why might people who prefer to be managers fail to out- perform people who were randomly chosen, some of whom did not want the job? We hypothesize that self-promoted managers are overconÞdent, especially about their social skills. Overcon- Þdence may lead managers to focus too much on their own be- havior at the expense of focusing on the skills and motivation of their teammates. We test this idea with exploratory analyses in which we Þrst assess overconÞdence on the group task. After the Þnal round of group tasks, we ask managers to reßect on whether they had performed much worse, worse, average, better, or much better than their peers. We computed an individual-level mea- sure of overconÞdence by regressing self-reported performance on each managerÕs causal contribution to the team ( α ) and capturing the residual. People who want to be in charge were much more overconÞdent than people who do not have strong preferences for being a manager ( d = 0 . 41 standard deviations, p < .01). These results align with Þeld studies on the overconÞdence of man- agers and executives (e.g., Malmendier and Tate 2015 ; Huffman, Raymond, and Shvets 2022 ). Although gender does not moderate the relationship between wanting to be in charge and overconÞ- dence, we Þnd that men are signiÞcantly more overconÞdent on average than women (the mean difference is 0.35 standard devi- ations, p = .02), in line with other evidence ( Exley and Kessler 2022 ; Tradenta, Neelim, and Vecci 2025 ). Random selection of managers will thus tend to result in the inclusion of more women (see also Goodall and Osterloh 2015 ). Second, we Þnd that self-promoted managers are particu- larly overconÞdent about their social skills. Among self-promoters we Þnd a strong negative correlation between self-reported peo- ple skills and performance on the RMET (correlation = − 0.37, p < .001). 26 This relationship was not signiÞcant for lottery man- agers. We focus primar- ily on the lottery managers, as the relationships between man- ager performance and broad skills/traits in the self-promoted arm are moderated by the Þlter of self-promotion. Only two measures clearly predict manager performance in the lottery arm: ßuid in- telligence (Ravens) and economic decision-making (assignment game). These associations are robust to a wide range of controls, including age, gender, education, and work experience, along with measures of emotional perceptiveness, personality traits, and risk aversion (see Online Appendix Table B.2 for details). Among self-promoted managers we Þnd negative correla- tions between management performance and both self-reported extraversion ( ρ = − 0 . 23 , p < .05) and self-reported political skill ( ρ = − 0 . 24 , p < .05). In other words, when managers are selected by self-promotion, the managers who think they are a Òpeople per- sonÓ are less successful in the job. III.D. Quantifying the Impact of Manager Selection Mechanisms in the Lab We quantify the beneÞts of skill-based promotions by com- paring the effect of different selection mechanisms on average manager contributions. In addition to comparing self-promoted and lottery managers, we use data from the lottery arm to sim- ulate counterfactuals in which managers are selected on speciÞc skills. 27 As an example, consider selecting managers based on the Pe- ter principle ( Peter and Hull 1969 ). In our case, this would mean ranking participants in terms of their individual production skills and appointing the top one-third of participants as managers (as one in three people in the experiment are managers). To esti- mate the average quality of managers under the Peter princi- ple, we rank participants in the lottery arm according to their scores on the individual tests of productivity (assessed before the group tests) and we identify the top tercile. The average manager quality among this group is an unbiased estimate of the average manager quality under a regime where managers are promoted 27. This subsection was not preregistered and is exploratory.
